key: Start with the question, then collect trustworthy data.
remember: A population is the full group; a sample is the part observed. A statistic estimates a population parameter.
apply: Measuring 30 randomly selected plots estimates yield for the field; measuring only the best plots introduces bias.

key: Check the source, year, unit and geographical coverage.
remember: Official figures answer different questions: area, production, yield and prices are not interchangeable.
apply: If production is 60 tonnes from 20 hectares, yield is 3 tonnes per hectare. Compare like units and reference years.

key: Match the graph to the variable.
remember: Bars compare categories; histograms show continuous distributions; an ogive shows cumulative frequency.
apply: With unequal histogram class widths, use frequency density so bar area represents frequency.

key: Choose the average for the question.
remember: Mean uses every value; median describes the middle; mode identifies the most frequent value or category.
apply: For yields 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, the mean is 6 but the median is 3. The unusually large yield pulls the mean upwards.

key: Additive amounts: AM. Growth factors: GM. Equal-distance speeds: HM.
remember: Use positive values for the usual AM ≥ GM ≥ HM relation. Convert growth percentages to factors before using GM.
apply: A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall gives factors 1.2 and 0.8: the final value is 0.96 of the start, not unchanged.

key: Report spread alongside the average.
remember: Variance has squared units; standard deviation has the original units. CV is useful only when a meaningful positive mean exists.
apply: Two crops can have the same mean yield and different variability. A smaller SD indicates more consistent yields on the same scale.

key: Describe asymmetry and tail behaviour separately.
remember: Skewness describes asymmetry. Kurtosis concerns tail weight relative to the normal distribution; it is not simply peak height.
apply: For a normal distribution, kurtosis β₂ = 3 and excess kurtosis = 0. State which convention you report.

key: Association measures a relationship, not a cause.
remember: Pearson correlation describes linear association; rank correlation works with ordered ranks. Always inspect the data plot.
apply: A correlation near zero can hide a strong curved relationship. Do not use it alone to conclude there is no relationship.

key: Regression predicts a response from an explanatory variable.
remember: The slope gives the change in predicted response for one unit of the predictor. A fitted line does not establish causation.
apply: If predicted yield = 2 + 0.04 × nitrogen, adding 10 units of nitrogen changes predicted yield by 0.4 units within the studied range.

key: Decide whether events overlap and whether they are independent.
remember: For a union, subtract the overlap. For an intersection, use a conditional probability unless independence is justified.
apply: If A and B are independent with probabilities 0.6 and 0.5, P(A and B) = 0.3 and P(A or B) = 0.8.

key: Select the distribution from the experiment.
remember: Binomial counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with constant probability; Poisson models counts under its assumptions.
apply: For 10 independent seeds each with germination probability 0.8, the expected number germinating is np = 8.

key: Sampling design determines how far results can be generalised.
remember: Random sampling controls selection; stratification samples within groups; clustering samples groups of units.
apply: To represent both irrigated and rainfed farms, stratify by irrigation status and randomly sample within each stratum.

key: State the hypotheses before looking at the test result.
remember: A p-value is a probability under the null model, not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
apply: At α = 0.05, p = 0.03 leads to rejection of H₀. A non-significant result means insufficient evidence, not proof of equality.

key: Standardise the estimate using its standard error.
remember: Check independence and the relevant large-sample approximation before applying a z test.
apply: For a population proportion test, check expected success and failure counts using the null proportion.

key: Choose the test from the study structure.
remember: Paired data require analysis of within-pair differences. Independent groups require an independent-samples method.
apply: Before-and-after measurements on the same plants are paired; they are not two independent samples.

key: Randomise, replicate and control local variation.
remember: Replication estimates experimental error; randomisation protects against systematic allocation bias; blocking reduces nuisance variation.
apply: Ten leaves measured on one treated plant are subsamples, not ten independently treated experimental units.

key: Use uniformity trials to study field heterogeneity.
remember: Grow a uniform crop and measure small basic units before deciding useful plot sizes, shapes and blocks.
apply: If fertility changes down the field, orient blocks to contain relatively similar plots rather than mixing the full gradient within each block.

key: ANOVA compares means through a variance ratio.
remember: A significant treatment F test indicates that not all treatment means are equal. It does not identify the differing pairs.
apply: For three treatments and 12 observations in a one-way CRD, treatment df = 2, error df = 9 and total df = 11.

key: Choose comparisons to match the scientific question.
remember: Account for multiplicity when examining many pairs. A significant omnibus test does not make every pair significant.
apply: Four treatment means produce six pairwise comparisons. Use a method suitable for the intended family of comparisons.

key: Choose the design to match field variation.
remember: CRD has no blocking; RBD controls one blocking factor; a Latin square controls row and column effects.
apply: With four treatments and three complete blocks, RBD treatment df = 3, block df = 2 and error df = 6.

key: Check interaction before interpreting main effects.
remember: A factorial experiment studies combinations of factor levels. Interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other.
apply: A fertiliser may increase yield under irrigation but show little benefit under drought: report those conditional effects.

key: Adjust for a relevant covariate measured before treatment.
remember: ANCOVA combines regression and ANOVA. Check linearity, comparable covariate slopes and the role of the covariate in the design.
apply: Initial plant height may improve precision when comparing final biomass; a measurement caused by the treatment needs different causal reasoning.

key: Estimate a missing plot; do not treat it as a new observation.
remember: Use the method appropriate to the design and reduce error degrees of freedom for estimated values.
apply: An RBD with one missing plot loses one error degree of freedom relative to the corresponding complete-data analysis.

key: Transform to address a model problem, not to force significance.
remember: Choose a transformation from the data scale and residual behaviour. Document it and interpret results on the appropriate scale.
apply: Log transformation turns multiplicative effects into additive ones, but log(0) is undefined. Any offset must be justified and reported.
